notes.body:
The passage counts letters and finds worlds in them. "A will, a command, by a saying" (إرادة أمر بقول) is twelve letters, and those twelve become twelve signs above and twelve below — the twelve constellations (البروج) in the sky and the twelve islands (الجزائر) on the earth. **The signs match because they spring from the same twelve letters**, one creative word written once in heaven and once in the ground beneath us.

But the witnesses do not match, and that is the real question. The heaven's twelve are attested by seven kingdoms — the seven climes (الأقاليم), the great regions into which the old world was mapped — while the earth's twelve are attested by seventeen seas. Above, the witnesses are few and gathered; below, many and scattered.

Picture a single lamp and its reflections. Held up in a still, high room, one flame throws a handful of clean reflections; carried down into a hall of broken mirrors, the same flame splinters into far more. *The light has not changed; only the surfaces have.* The heaven is the world nearer the inward, where meaning is one and its signs stay gathered; the earth is the outward world, where that same meaning shatters into a crowd of witnesses.

This is the rule the Master gives as the chapter closes: **the inward is one, and its witnesses in the outward are many**, "because of the abundance of the likenesses and the breadth of the sacred laws." Seven belongs to the sky because seven is the number of the higher order that governs from above — the seven speakers, the seven heavens. Seventeen belongs to the sea because the outward multiplies; water spreads and divides where light stays single.

So seven above and seventeen below over the same twelve is no mismatch. We are watching one truth descend — kept whole and few in the heaven of meaning, broken into many bright witnesses on the earth of form.
etymology: برج (constellation): from the root ب-ر-ج, to rise high and stand out — which also gives the word for a tower. A constellation is a tower of stars, a conspicuous house in the sky that the sun is seen to enter and leave.

جزيرة (island): from the root ج-ز-ر, to cut off or sever; the same root gives جَزْر, the ebbing of the tide. An island is land the water has cut away and set apart, encircled and defined by the sea around it.

شاهد (witness): from the root ش-ه-د, to be present and to testify to what one has seen. A witness is not hearsay but something present that vouches for another — the seas and kingdoms stand present, attesting to the signs.

إقليم (clime, kingdom): a region of the earth, an early borrowing into Arabic from the Greek word for a zone or slope of the world, kept as one of the seven great bands into which the inhabited earth was divided.

notes.body:
The puzzle dissolves once we notice that the two counts are counting two different things, not the same phrase twice. Both point back to the very same act of creation; they simply give it two different faces.

The first count listens to the divine utterance itself. When Allah wills a thing, the word He speaks is كُن فَيَكُون — Be, and it is. Spell that spoken word out and it carries seven letters, and so **seven foundational things branch out of it**: the air, then water, darkness and light, then smoke, the condensing of heat, and fire. The seven letters are the seven bones of creation.

The second count spells out instead the names of the three inner movements behind the utterance — إِرَادَة (a will), then أَمْر (a command), then بِقَوْل (by a saying). Written out, those three names carry twelve letters, and so **twelve signs are drawn across the sky**: the twelve constellations, each a marker of one of those twelve letters.

Think of a single order a captain gives. We can count the letters of the command he shouts, or the letters in the words that name his intention, his instruction, and his speech. It is one event, tallied two ways.

So there is no contradiction, only one creative act read at two depths: heard as an utterance it yields seven, unfolded into its inner names it yields twelve — seven principles below and twelve signs above, both flowing from the one will that says كُن.
etymology: كُن (Be): from the root ك-و-ن, to be or to come into existence, the command form of كَانَ. The word for the whole cosmos, كَوْن, grows from this same root, so the word that summons existence and the word for existence itself are one family.

حَرْف (letter): from the root ح-ر-ف, an edge, brink, or margin. A حَرْف is the edge of a sound, its smallest cut, which is why counting حُرُوف is really counting the edges from which larger words are assembled.

بُرْج (constellation): from the root ب-ر-ج, to be high, prominent, to tower up. A بُرْج is a tower or fortress, so a constellation is read as a tower of light standing tall in the sky — a raised, unmistakable sign.
